title: Central Limit Theorem Simulator MicroSim
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Data Science
description: Draw repeated samples from a normal, uniform, right-skewed, or bimodal population and compare the histogram of sample means with the normal curve that the central limit theorem predicts.

educational.topic: Central limit theorem and standard error
learningObjectives: Students will be able to compare the distribution of sample means with the population distribution and analyze how the sample size changes its shape and spread.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Simulation that compares a population with the distribution of its sample means on a shared axis
keyQuestions: How does the shape of the histogram of sample means differ from the shape of the population?
What happens to the spread of the sample means when n goes from 10 to 100?
For which population does the bell shape need the largest sample size to appear, and why?
commonMisconceptions: The central limit theorem says the data become normal when the sample is large (the population keeps its shape, and it is the distribution of sample means that becomes normal).
Taking more samples makes the sample means less spread out (the spread depends on the sample size n, and more samples only fill in the histogram).
The standard error is the same as the standard deviation of the data (it is σ/√n, the standard deviation of the sample mean).
A sample size of 30 always guarantees a normal shape (strongly skewed populations need larger samples).
assessmentOpportunities: Students predict the mean and the standard deviation of the sample means for samples of size 25 from a population with μ = 80 and σ = 20, and explain whether the histogram of those sample means would look normal if the population were strongly skewed.
